# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. A bare "ok", "yes", or "looks good" is not "keep going": when it is the owner's whole message and this chat asked him nothing, start no work and ask what he wants. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line in the reply, not only in a progress line, before other work. Use the CLI's own words for what changed; do not guess at a cause it does not name.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. Setup is not a work item: never create one for setup steps. Owner setup steps go in the reply; only a step doctor checks (trust the hooks in Codex, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", marked as a setup step, and leaves it once doctor stops reporting it. "Start a new session" goes in the reply only. "New work", "track", "work item", or "done properly" always makes an item. When the owner names a deliverable but not what it should say or do ("write a short project brief"), create the item, add the content question as `Q-01` with the item waiting on him, and ask it in the reply before building anything; never fill the content in yourself. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way, titled in the owner's words (say the title in one line), and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --text '<his exact words>'`
4. An item that shows `delivery: not-offered` once it reaches stage 03 or later, an item the briefing lists with the agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer", or an owner who hands the goal over in his own words ("you drive"): open `work-delegate` first. It is the only skill that makes the offer, and it records owner-led at once for a small item. Never ask the offer here. When it asks the offer, wait for his answer before building. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load`, or the owner answered the questions that set them, or asked for it done properly: `work-requirements`, which shows them to him for approval. A change the owner asks for to a requirement (`R-xx`), at any stage: `work-requirements`. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so in the final reply, not a progress line ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. An item that changes committed files goes through stage 07 (its own worktree), never onto the default branch. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the table and checkbox format in this skill's own `references/planning.md` (the `references/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`; read it first): each task's `**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`, `**Done when:**`, and `**Depends on:**` on its own line. Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, with the item's own id prefix in lower case (`wi-007-...` for WI-007, `tv2-007-...` for TV2-007; the show command in step 2 prints the branch and folder to use); in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. Commit with files staged by name and a plain message with no AI credit: no `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason), because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks. Refused without asking: show him the exact command, ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting on the owner. Never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, validation is clean, and the current focus names the item and its real next step (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").
   `toolkit work history <id> --note '<what changed>'`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, for example `claude/wi-007-csv-export`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See this skill's own `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.

# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.

# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.

# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.

# Trackers

A project has exactly one tracker. `.toolkit.json` names it in
`tracker.type`. Read it with:

```text
toolkit config get tracker.type
```

| `tracker.type` | Where items live | How skills work with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | `.work-items/` in the main checkout, one folder per item | `toolkit work ...` commands |
| `notion` | The project's own Work Items database in Notion, under the "AI Agent Second Brain" page | `toolkit work ...` commands (the CLI calls Notion) |
| `github` | GitHub Issues in the project's repository | Written instructions: [trackers/github.md](trackers/github.md) |
| `jira` | Jira issues in the project's Jira project | Written instructions: [trackers/jira.md](trackers/jira.md) |

## Rules for every tracker

- The same model everywhere: the fourteen stages, the six statuses, the
  `WORK-ITEM.md` body, and one design per item. `toolkit work lifecycle`
  prints the stages, statuses, types, and approval gates.
- Never create a second tracker, and never keep a local copy of items that
  live in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.
- A sub-item is its own item with its own requirements, design, roadmap,
  and approvals. Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Only the main agent changes a work item. Agents return findings; the main
  agent saves them.
- Read every change back.

## Local and Notion

- Every read and write goes through `toolkit work ...`. The commands behave
  the same for both.
- Local: a folder nested inside an item's folder is a sub-item. A plain folder
  with no record in it is a group. `archive/` hides items from the briefing
  and from `toolkit work next`. The project's rule for this tracker is
  `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md`.
- Notion: the design is the item's "Solution Design" child page. A card the
  owner made with Notion's New button has no template body; the CLI fills it
  on its next read and reports it. A Stage the owner changed by dragging is
  kept, and Status follows it.
- Writes outside the "AI Agent Second Brain" page are refused by the CLI.
  Never work around that.

## GitHub Issues and Jira

- `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3 and print the path of the written
  instructions. Follow those instructions instead.
- The work-item hooks do nothing for these trackers, so the skill must keep
  the item correct by itself: read it back after every change.
- Create nothing in GitHub or Jira that setup did not already approve (labels,
  fields, workflows). Creating and updating issues for work items is part of
  normal work once the tracker was chosen.

## Templates for every tracker

The templates come from the model project. The toolkit plugin carries an exact
copy of the model in its `scaffold/model/` folder, so every project can reach
them, whatever its tracker:

- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`: the work item
  body. A new GitHub issue body or Jira description starts from it, from
  `## Overview` to the end.
- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md`: the design. A new
  design comment starts from it, without its frontmatter.

The file `~/.config/toolkit-v2/plugin-root` holds the path of the toolkit
plugin's folder (every session start refreshes it). The `scaffold/model/`
folder is inside that folder. A local project also has its own copies in
`.work-items/work-item-template/`, which the CLI prefers, so a project that
edited its template keeps its version. Both files open with a fill-in guide
comment: follow it, then delete it.

# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command, in both hosts (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Text goes on standard input in Claude Code and in single quotes or a
  `mktemp -d` file in Codex, never in double quotes and never at a fixed name
  such as `/tmp/wi001.md` ("Text in a command", below).
- Ask the owner in the reply text. Never ask through a question tool (such as
  Codex's `request_user_input`): he may never see it, and the reply must hold
  the question.
- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never
  report a refused or failed fetch as a blocker.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.
- Keep the current focus current when an item's stage or next step changes
  ("The current focus", below).

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`. The
  agent-led delivery offer is the one exception: only `work-delegate` makes
  the offer and records its answer.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Codex matches
  its command rule against the plain command.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc, "Text in a command" below).
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The new text is the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes. Leave out the section's
  fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the section holds real content.
  `<file>` below is `-` (standard input) in Claude Code ("Text in a command").

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A title is the owner's call. A new item's title uses the owner's own words
  for the request. When you shorten them or choose another, say the title in
  one line in the reply ("I started WI-003, 'Write a short project brief'.").
  To retitle an item, say the new title to him in one line before
  `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still prints "Saved". So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Write an apostrophe inside them as `'\''`, for example
  `--note 'Owner'\''s words: "ship it"'`. Never use double quotes for text.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere. Claude Code
  refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary folder there could never be
  deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text,
  make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so
  two sessions or two projects never share a file), write the file in it with
  the file edit tool (`apply_patch`), run the `toolkit` command alone with the
  file's full path, and delete the file and the folder right after the command
  succeeds (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner
  anything. Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell
  command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  ```

- Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project
  starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item.
- Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
  file there confuses the design lookup.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note '<text>' --effect '<what it changes>'`
when (without `--effect`, the row says which skill continues the item):

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

A note that quotes the owner's approval ("Owner's words: ...") right after an
approval or a `waiting_on` change gets its own `--effect` that says what the
answer changes ("Result approved; work-finish continues."). Without it, the
row's default effect is worked out from the item before the change and can
name the wrong next step.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## The current focus

The current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) is the first thing the next session
reads. Its "Now" section names work item ids and titles, never their status;
its "Next session starts with" section says where to resume. A line there that
names a step already done misleads every later session.

When an item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the focus
does not say, read the focus and check two things before the reply ends:

- "Now" lists the item (id and title only). Add it when it is missing; take
  it off when the item is Done or Cancelled.
- "Next session starts with" does not name a step that is done or no longer
  next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
  points at the item ("Continue WI-012 from its Resume here: build P1.").

Also drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once `toolkit doctor` no
longer reports it. Change the "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and keep
the `# Current focus` title line. Leave every other line as it is. Save the
whole text back with the version you read, so another session's change is not
lost (`--expect` refuses a stale save with exit code 2: read it again and
redo the change). Claude Code passes the text on standard input.

```text
toolkit memory focus --json
toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
```

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. The work item itself stays
the record of where the item stands.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work. The CLI writes the history rows for a
hand move itself: "Moved by hand", "Folder renamed by hand", or "Parent
changed in Notion by hand" on the item, and "Sub-item ... moved out" or
"moved here" on the parents it left and joined. Add a note only for what the
CLI cannot know, such as the owner's reason.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses. `<prefix>` is the item's own id
  prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`, `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for
  `ACME-007`. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name,
  so a branch named `wi-001-...` for `TV2-001` is not linked to it.
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
  A commit message never carries a `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI or a
  "Generated with" line. Stage files by name; never `git add -A`, `git add .`,
  or `git commit -a`.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one.
  - Run each Git write as its own command and ask for escalated permissions:
    set `sandbox_permissions` to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason
    that says what the command does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own
    branch."). An approval without escalation still runs the command inside
    the sandbox, where it fails on `.git/index.lock`.
  - Tell the owner in one line what the command does before Codex asks.
  - Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy, but
    AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
    step, show the owner the exact command, ask him to approve it in an
    interactive session or to run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting
    on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.
  - Never work around it: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
    `.git/`, no building on the default branch instead of the item's branch.
- The project's shared-repository rule runs `git fetch origin` before the
  first edit. When `git remote` prints nothing, the project has no remote:
  never run `git fetch`, and never report a refused or failed fetch as a
  blocker or write it into the item. Check `git remote` before any fetch.
  Without a remote there is no pull request and no push: the item's branch is
  merged locally (`work-finish`), and documents are committed locally
  (`publish-docs` does this by itself).
- A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it, then commit with a message you
  write (`git commit -m 'Merge <branch>: <what it brings>'`), never
  `git commit --no-edit`, which keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the
  message.

# Planning and building a work item

Detail for `work-on` steps 6 to 10. Carried over from Toolkit V1's lifecycle
and planning rules, with V2 names.

## Roadmap and tasks

- The Roadmap is an ordered list of phases from where the item stands to the
  finished result. Name phases to fit the work. They do not have to match the
  fourteen lifecycle stages. "Phase" (`P1`) is the item's plan; "stage"
  (`08-build`) is the lifecycle. Never mix the two words.
- Build the phases from the approved design's "Build and verification plan"
  (its Technical sequence and Acceptance checks), and from the chosen
  option's Build order. With no design (a small item that skipped design with
  a recorded reason), build them from the requirements.
- Each phase has one or more tasks, one or more sub-items, or both.
- Keep detail in proportion to the item. A one-hour fix needs one phase with
  one or two tasks.
- Link sources; do not copy them. A task names the `R-xx` it implements and
  the design section it follows.

Roadmap section format, from the work item template (the table keeps these
columns in every tracker, and the phase name follows an em dash, as in the
template):

```markdown
A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.

| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 — CSV export button | The export button creates a file | In Progress | The file opens in Excel with every column | None. |
| P2 — Large exports | Exports over 10,000 rows finish | Not Started | A 50,000-row export finishes in under a minute | WI-015 |
```

Tasks section format. Each phase gets a `###` heading with the same phase ID
and name as its Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,
`**Done when:**`, `**Depends on:**`) starts its own line, and every line of a
task but the last ends with two spaces, which Markdown reads as a line break.
Never run the fields together on one line:

```markdown
### P1 — CSV export button

- [ ] **P1-T01 — Add the export endpoint** · In Progress  
  **Work:** Add the endpoint that streams the report rows as CSV (R-01, design Technical sequence step 1).  
  **Deliverable:** The endpoint and its tests.  
  **Done when:** The endpoint test passes and a manual export opens in Excel.  
  **Depends on:** None.
```

Phase status words: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase
that was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned". From stage 07 on,
`toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no phase table, when Tasks
has no checkbox lines, and when a template example row or task is left. When
the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.

# WI-001: Build tally word count CLI — solution design

**Requirements:** WI-001 R-01 and R-02  
**Design status:** Approved  
**Requirements checked:** WI-001 R-01 and R-02, 2026-09-28  
**Last updated:** 2026-09-28  
**Design approval:** Approved by Mike on 2026-09-28

## What this design solves

Mike runs a command on a named text file and sees one integer: the word count by default, or the line count with --lines. WI-001 delivers word mode; its child WI-002 delivers line mode.

## Requirements and design readiness

Both requirements are Finalized in WI-001. An independent requirements review found no material gap.

| Requirement | Delivery item | Design coverage |
|---|---|---|
| R-01 — Word count by default | WI-001 | Option A word mode |
| R-02 — Line count with --lines | WI-002 | Option A line mode |

## What exists today

The repository had no application code when the design was proposed on 2026-09-28. It has a test plan template but no bin directory.

## Constraints and assumptions

- Run as node bin/tally.js <file-path> or node bin/tally.js --lines <file-path>, as Mike approved in the starting request.
- Use plain Node.js with no npm packages and node:test checks, per the recorded project preference.
- Files are ordinary UTF-8 text files that fit in memory. This is an approved Option A assumption.

## Design options

### Option A — One Node.js command

Create bin/tally.js with built-in argument handling and file reading. Accept exactly a path, or --lines followed by a path. Reject missing or extra arguments, repeated --lines, unknown flags, and flags after the path. Read the file as UTF-8. Print one integer and a line break on success. Print a short error to standard error and exit nonzero for invalid arguments or file errors.

Word mode splits on runs of spaces or line breaks, discards empty pieces, and returns 0 for an empty file. Tabs are not word separators. Line mode counts LF, CR, and CRLF breaks, treating CRLF as one break; add one for a nonempty final segment. Blank lines count, a trailing break adds no extra line, and an empty file returns 0.

Hold the text in memory for one run. Read with the user's file permissions and never execute contents. tests/tally.test.js uses node:test, built-in assertions, and temporary files. A whole-file read may use too much memory for a large file; the approved scope is ordinary text files.

**Build order:** WI-001 adds word mode and its checks. WI-002 starts from that code and adds line mode and its checks.

## Recommendation and owner decision

**Recommendation:** Option A, one plain Node.js command with no package dependency.  
**Owner decision:** Mike approved Option A on 2026-09-28.  
**Reason for decision:** Mike's approval followed the proposal and its independent requirements and design reviews. He also requested that --lines be delivered by a sub-item.

## Selected design

Option A is selected. WI-001 and WI-002 deliver its modes separately.

### End-to-end flow

1. Mike runs node bin/tally.js notes.txt for words or node bin/tally.js --lines notes.txt for lines.
2. The command checks the exact accepted argument form before reading.
3. It reads UTF-8 text, calculates the requested count, and prints one integer with a line break.
4. Invalid arguments or read failures print a short error to standard error and exit nonzero.

### Components and responsibilities

- bin/tally.js owns argument parsing, file reading, counting, output, and errors.
- tests/tally.test.js checks both modes and invalid input using node:test and temporary files.
- WI-001 adds the default mode; WI-002 extends the same files with --lines.

### Data, access, and integration details

The command reads one named local file using the caller's permissions. It keeps text in memory for one run and stores nothing. It uses built-in Node.js modules only.

### Edge cases and failure behavior

Empty files print 0 in both modes. Repeated spaces and line breaks do not add words. Tabs are not separators for words. Blank lines count. A final nonempty line counts without a trailing break, while a trailing break adds no extra line. CRLF is one break. Reject unknown, repeated, misplaced, missing, and extra arguments. File errors go to standard error with nonzero exit.

### Release and ongoing operation

No service, database, migration, package installation, or deployment is needed. Run the command with Node.js. A larger-file requirement would need a separate design change.

## Build and verification plan

### Technical sequence

1. WI-001: implement default word mode and argument/file errors in bin/tally.js.
2. WI-001: add node:test checks for sample, repeated separators, empty file, and error paths; run a manual word-count command.
3. WI-002: start from the completed WI-001 code and implement --lines, including LF, CR, and CRLF.
4. WI-002: add checks for blank lines, trailing break, final nonempty line, empty file, invalid flag use, and a manual --lines command.

### Acceptance checks

| Requirement or acceptance item | Verification method | Expected result | Evidence location |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-01 | node:test and manual sample, repeated separator, and empty-file runs | Counts match WI-001 R-01 | WI-001 test output and review |
| R-02 | node:test and manual blank, trailing-break, final-line, CRLF, and empty-file runs | Counts match WI-001 R-02 | WI-002 test output and review |
| Argument and file errors | node:test invalid argument and missing-file runs | Error on standard error and nonzero exit | Test output |

## Diagrams

The command has one path: parse arguments, read the named file, count words or lines, then print the number. No separate components or shared state need a diagram.

## Sources and decisions that affect the build

| Claim or decision | Source | Date | Evidence type | Checked how |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Default word and --lines behavior | WI-001 R-01, R-02, Q-01, Q-02 | 2026-09-28 | Owner decision | Requirements approval in WI-001 |
| Option A selected and scope split | Mike in chat | 2026-09-28 | Owner decision | Approval and history in WI-001; WI-002 created with --covers R-02 |
| No application code existed | Repository scan | 2026-09-28 | Project evidence | No bin directory or application source found |
| Plain Node.js and node:test preference | Project memory | 2026-09-28 | Project evidence | Session briefing |

## Where a builder could misread this design

- Repeated separators add no words; tabs are not word separators.
- Blank lines count, a trailing break adds no line, and a final nonempty line counts.
- CRLF is one line break.
- Print only the integer and a line break, with no label.
- --lines must appear once before the path.
- WI-002 delivers R-02; it inherits the approved parent requirement and design.

- The checker is independent: never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.

- The approval covers the result shown. It is not an approval to merge, deploy, or publish; `work-finish` handles those.
- "Looks good" to a question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.

Also checks a build plan before the build when asked. Never the agent that built it; changes nothing.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash

# Acceptance checker

Check whether a finished result does what the owner asked. You are never the
agent that built it. You run tests and read code, but you change nothing. You
advise; the main agent fixes; the owner approves.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the requirements (Agreed goal, every
  `R-xx` with its acceptance check, the Acceptance list), the design's
  Acceptance checks table (in its "Build and verification plan") and the
  "How to check it" column of the selected option's Requirement coverage, the
  item's test plan when it has one (a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md`),
  the branch or commit to check, and the project's test commands.
- Check that you are looking at the exact code the brief names:

  ```text
  git status
  git rev-parse HEAD
  git log --oneline -5
  ```

  If the commit differs from the one in the brief, say so first.
- When the brief asks for a check before a merge, report the exact commit
  you checked, so the main agent can confirm nothing changed after it.

## Check

- Run the project's tests and every acceptance check you can run. Copy each
  command and its result line exactly.
- For each requirement, give one verdict:
  - **Met:** the acceptance check passed, or the evidence shows the required
    behavior. Name the evidence.
  - **Partly met:** some of the behavior works. Say what is missing.
  - **Not met:** the behavior is missing or wrong. Say what you saw.
  - **Not run:** the check could not run here. Say why and what would run it.
    Never report a check that did not run as passed.
- Read the diff for the item's branch against its base. Report defects you
  see: broken edge cases, missing error handling the requirements ask for,
  behavior the requirements did not ask for, files changed that the design
  did not name, and anything that would ship something unfinished.
- Walk the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Report any
  step where it breaks, even when each requirement passes on its own.

## Plan check (only when the brief asks for one)

Before a build starts, the brief may give the item's Roadmap and Tasks, the
requirements, and the design's "Build and verification plan" instead of a
finished result.
Then check the plan, not code:

- Every `R-xx` is covered by at least one task, and every task's "Done when"
  names evidence someone else can check.
- Each task has one owner, and each file has one writer. "Depends on" is
  right: no task starts before what it needs.
- Tasks that run at the same time have clear boundaries: no two builders
  write the same file, and no two use the same shared environment (a sandbox
  org, a database, a test service) at the same time without a stated order.
- No task relies on something the design or the code no longer says.
- Changes that affect other work items are named.

A different phase structure is not a defect by itself. Work that runs in
parallel does not need one agent per phase. Return for a plan check: the
verdict (ready to build, or not ready) in one line, then each finding with
the task id, what is wrong, and the fix in one line.

## Boundaries

- Bash is for tests and read-only commands only: running tests, `git status`,
  `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, listing files. Never edit, stage, commit,
  push, merge, deploy, install, or delete anything.
- Never run a command against a shared or production org or service. Never
  touch production data.
- Never run a `toolkit` command that writes. Do not edit the work item.
- Do not start other agents. Do not ask the owner anything.

## Return (result check)

1. **Verdict:** ready for the owner, or not ready, in one line, with the
   commit checked.
2. **Per requirement:** a table with the `R-xx`, the verdict, and the evidence
   or the gap in one line.
3. **Tests run:** each command and its exact result line.
4. **Defects in the diff:** each with the file and line, what is wrong, and
   the fix in one line. "None found" when there are none.
5. **Not run:** each check that could not run, and why.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every file, function, and setting.
Short sentences, one idea each. No figurative or metaphorical language, no
idioms, no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep
every number, path, and command output exactly as found. Lead with the
verdict and keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion). Text: one-line values (`--description`, `--source`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)` and drop that text. A record body, the focus, or the glossary: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--body-file -` or `--set-file -`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), never through a file; in Codex give it in single quotes (`--body '<text>'`, `--text '<text>'`), or write a file with the file edit tool in a new folder made with `mktemp -d`, run the `toolkit` command alone with that file, and delete the file and the folder right after. Never write the file and run the command in one shell command, and never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate. The save command checks too: when memory already has a record with the same key or a very similar description or text, it saves nothing, exits with code 2, and lists those records. Read each one with the second command below, which prints its `version` field. The same fact: save that record's type and slug again with `--expect <version>`, which updates it (the first 12 characters of the version are enough; for a record with the same key, the command's own fix line already gives them). A newer fact that replaces it: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A different fact: say why in one line and save again with `--allow-similar`. Never add `--allow-similar` without reading the listed records.
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. An unanswered "Save to memory?" (his next message does not answer it, or the session is ending) is not dropped: save it as a proposal (`--proposal`, never with an approver). A proposal is not a fact: search leaves it out, the agent does not rely on it, and the decision list shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it through `work-decide`.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body with the model's bold labels, each starting its own paragraph: `**Remember:**`, `**Why:**` (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), `**How to apply:**`, `**Evidence and limits:**` (the source and an absolute date), `**Related memories:**` (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), `**Authoritative records:**`. Never write them as `## headings`. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again, with `--expect <version>` (the `version` field of the step 2 read), updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A better name or a type that matches the content: rename it; links to it are repaired. The first form is for the owner's approval (his words or his yes); the second for a routine save in `trusted` mode; the third for an unanswered proposal; the fourth updates a record read in step 2. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus with its version, change it, write the whole text back. The model's format: the `# Current focus` title line, a "Last updated" line (date, source, who), and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status; keep the title and the date line (the CLI adds them when missing, but without the source and who). Drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once doctor no longer reports it. On a new project remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." (a proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."). A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses. End the reply with the question still waiting for him, if there is one, or those exact words.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Proposals and declined saves

- A proposal saved in step 3 waits for the owner's yes or no; `work-decide` asks him. His answer in this chat also settles it: yes approves it (a current record with him as the approver), no rejects it (the proposal is deleted).
  `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
  `toolkit memory reject <key>`
- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it (a saved proposal: reject it). Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record, and never propose it again under other words. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
